translations.text: The life and conduct of the holy Apa Eustathius, the general of Emperor Trajan, and Theopiste his wife, and Agapius and Theopistus his sons, who completed their struggle in the great city of Rome on the twentieth day of the month of Thoth, under Emperor Trajan. In peace. Amen.
A place of instruction is established for holy people,
belonging to nature and to free choice, both together, on their part [?],

achieving virtue and wishing to instruct those around him through the others who have lived from the beginning, those who receive grace from him, the benefactor of us all from the beginning, our God and our Lord Jesus Christ.
These are the things he commands and asks of us—
I am speaking of gratitude.

We are those whom he benefits and [?] sustains. There are also many teachings and deeds of strong and blessed people set down for us in the holy Scriptures, like living images, so that those who wish to follow them may emulate their honorable achievements and not fall short of them in their strength.
For my part, those about whom I will now write to you are people who achieved virtue in our own times, who do not fall short in their achievements or their strength.

The people of old, about whom accounts were written in the holy Scriptures [?], so that those who hear may love what is good, and so that those who say, “It is impossible to live rightly now, in these last times,” may themselves turn to the strength of their virtues.
But I say that, for someone who wishes to do good,
the hardship of the times and a troubled existence cannot hinder a life intent on accomplishing good deeds.
If someone wishes first to follow the principle of nature and the teachings of the holy people of whom we have spoken,
he will find ease on the path of a life full of virtue, after the pattern of these things now set before me.

Let us speak about them and write to you about the beginning of their lives and the reason their path was honored, through the things that happened to us. Let us reveal them to you, and may you yourselves listen to them willingly, without any unbelief
or hesitation, O blessed people and servants of Christ.
Now, during the reign of Emperor Trajan, when idol worship was widespread, there rose to power
a general whose name was Placidas. He was close to the emperor and was especially honored for his family background by the standards of this world. He was also extremely wealthy,
surpassing all the nobles of the palace in possessions, gold and silver, numerous slaves, and other property.
He was a pagan in his religion, but he was adorned with deeds of righteousness.
He helped those who were afflicted,
giving assistance to those who were treated unjustly. He clothed the naked and fed the hungry.
He also rescued many who had been condemned to death, using his own money.
In short, he provided for everyone in need according to their bodily needs.
He became a new Cornelius in that time.
He had a wife, and she too worshiped idols.
But she was likewise adorned with every good deed.
They had two sons.
They brought these up too in the same way, with good intentions.
The man was very well known for the good deeds he did.
He was also famous for his strength, so that the barbarians were afraid whenever they heard even his name, because he was an outstanding warrior.
He distinguished himself in every battle.
His whole passion was simply to hunt wild animals and excel at it.
But God, who is good and loves everyone everywhere who honors him, did not overlook that man's good deeds.
Nor did he wish to let his good intentions come to nothing.
Rather, as it is written, “In every nation, anyone who fears the Lord and practices righteousness is accepted by him.”
Since God has abundant tender compassion, he was pleased to save him in the following way, which we shall recount.
One day he went to hunt wild animals in the mountains, as was his custom.
He and his troops went, with all his servants accompanying him.
A herd of deer appeared to him, grazing.
He ordered his troops to pursue the animals.
While the whole company of soldiers was busy catching the animals,
one of them appeared that was beautiful
and taller than all the others. It separated from the herd and came out.
It ran into the wooded areas in the rugged mountains, where it was difficult to walk.
When Placidus saw it,
he wanted to catch it.
He took some soldiers with him, left all the rest, and ran after it.
Those who had gone with him grew tired and gave up, but he pressed on alone in pursuit.
By God's providence, however, he did not grow tired, nor did the horse he was riding give up in the rugged terrain.
After pursuing it for a long time, he emerged far away from his troops.
Then that animal stood on a very high mountain.
When the commander approached him, with no one beside him, he stood looking in every direction.
He was considering how he could catch it.
And God, who loves humanity, who [?] the salvation of human beings in many ways,
caused him to be caught by this means, through his own strategy, as Cornelius was through Peter, and as Paul was when he appeared to him while he was persecuting him.

After a long time had passed, while Placidus stood looking at the animal, marveling at its great size and wondering how he would catch it, the Lord showed him a sign of this kind so that he could see him.
He appeared to him in this way:
There was a sign of the cross between its antlers,
shining more brightly than the sun.
Also, between its antlers, he appeared in the likeness of the body that God wore in the womb of the Virgin,
and that he put on for our salvation.
He called to Placidus in a human voice from the animal, saying:
“O Placidus, why are you chasing me?”
“For it is for your sake that I have appeared to you through this animal.
For I am Jesus, whom you serve without knowing him.
The good deeds that you do have come before me.
That is why I have revealed myself to you,
and I have hunted you through this irrational animal,
and caught you in the nets of my divinity.
It is not right for those who love me through their good deeds to be slaves to unclean demons and to idols that are dead, blind, and without perception.
That is why I came down to earth in this form in which you see me, wishing to save the human race.”
When Placidus heard these things, he was afraid and fell to the ground.
After a long time had passed, he got up by himself, wanting to understand precisely the miracle that had appeared.
And he said, “What, then, is this vision that I have seen?”
“And what kind of voice is this that I have heard?”
“Reveal yourself to me, you who are speaking with me, so that I may believe in you.”
The Lord said to him, “Take courage, Placidus.”
“I am Jesus Christ, the Son of the living God, who created heaven and earth when they did not exist.”
“I created all matter, which is beyond counting.”
“I am the one who revealed the light and separated it from the darkness.
I am the one who made the sun to shine by day,
and appointed the moon and the stars to shine by night.
I am the one who appointed the times, the seasons, and the days.
I am the one who formed the human being from the earth.
I appeared upon it in the flesh that I took on for the salvation of humanity.
I am the one who was crucified. I died, was buried, and rose from the dead on the third day.

When Placidus heard these things, he fell on his face and cried out, “I believe in the Lord, for you are the one who created everything and who brings back those who are wandering and those who have gone astray.
And you are the one who brings the dead back to life.”
The Lord answered, “If you believe, go and make your way to the chief priests of the Christians, and seek grace from them through baptism.”
Placidus answered him, “Lord, give me permission to tell these things to my wife and my children, so that they too may believe in you.”
The Lord said to him, “Tell them.
And cleanse yourselves of defilement by receiving the seal of baptism. Then return to this place, and I will reveal myself to you and tell you the mystery of salvation.”
Then Placidus came down from the mountain.
He went into his house.
When evening came, he began telling his wife and his children what he had seen in the vision and how the Lord had appeared to him.
His wife immediately cried out, “My lord, my brother, you have seen the God who was crucified, whom the Christians worship!”
For he alone is the true God, who saves those who put their hope in him.
And she cried out loudly, saying, “Have mercy on me, Lord Jesus Christ, and on my two children as well!”
And she said to her husband, “Last night I too saw him. He said to me, ‘Tomorrow you, your husband, and your children will come to me.’

And I recognized that he is God, Jesus Christ, the God of the Galileans. He wants to reveal himself to you through such a miracle, by means of an animal, so that you will be amazed at his power and believe in him.
“Come now, during the night, and let us go and receive baptism from the chief priests of the Christians, as he commanded you.”
For through this, those who believe in him become members of his household.”
Placidus answered, “This is what the one who appeared to me told me.”
At midnight they secretly took their two children and a few of their servants.
They went to the chief priest of the Christians and told him the entire vision.
They professed their belief in the Lord Jesus Christ.
They begged him to give them the seal of Christ through baptism.
He rejoiced and gave glory to God, who wants everyone to live and to come to the knowledge of the truth.
The chief priest received them, instructed them, and entrusted to them the holy mysteries of the faith. He baptized them in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
He named Placidus Eustace, and his wife Theopiste. Of his children, he named the older one Agapius and the younger one Theopistus.
He gave them a share of the precious body and blood of Christ and sent them away.
He said to them, “May God, Christ, be with you
and grant you his kingdom forever.”
Know that the hand of the Lord is with you.
And I beg you, when you are in paradise, to remember the soul of John, this poor man, the least of all.
When morning came, Eustathius took some horses.
He went to the mountain and approached the place where he had seen the vision.
He sent the soldiers of the hunting party to hunt the animals.
But he stayed alone for a little while.
Afterward, he set off.
He approached the place where he had first seen the image.
He fell on his face and cried out, saying, “Lord, I have understood that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God, and I have believed in you, your good Father, and the Holy Spirit.
Now, therefore, I beg you:
if you have made me worthy of the holy grace of your divinity, explain to me the things you told me.”
Immediately the Lord answered and said to him, “Blessed are you, Placidus, because you have received the fullness of grace.
You have clothed yourself in incorruptibility, which lasts forever.
Now, therefore, the work of your faith has become evident.
For the devil will envy you because you have abandoned him.
He will strive to use every trick and fight against you.
For you must bear many trials.
If you endure them, you will receive your crown of victory.
Look, until now you have risen very high in the affairs of this life and in temporary wealth.
Become rich also in spiritual exaltation.
Do not grow weak now or lose heart over the glory of this world that you had before.
Rather, just as you proved yourself mighty among people, fighting and striving to please a mortal king, strive in the same way to be a mighty man against the devil and preserve your faith for me.
I am the immortal King.”
For another Job must arise in these times, one who will overcome the devil in the trial.
Watch yourself, lest a blasphemous thought rise in your heart.
But when you have been brought low, I will come to you and restore your former glory.
And when the Lord had said these things to him,
he went up to heaven.
The Lord said to him, “Eustathius, willingly accept the trial that has been appointed for you in your last days.”

And Eustathius said, “If this is the end of my days, I beg you, my Lord: if it is impossible for the things you have now decreed for me to pass without happening to me, command us to accept our trial.
But give us strength, Lord God of hosts, for it is in you that we trust.”
The Lord said to him, “Struggle on, Eustathius. My grace will guard your hearts.”
Then Saint Eustathius came down from the mountain.
He went to his house and told his wife what the Lord had said to him.
They bent their knees together.
They prayed, saying, “Lord, may your will be done.”
After a few days, a plague broke out in his household, and all his servants died.
When this happened, Eustathius recognized the trial, just as he had been told beforehand that it would happen to him. He accepted it joyfully, encouraging his wife not to lose heart.
A little while later, all his horses and livestock also died.
And in the same way he accepted this other trial with joy.
After these things, he left his house with his wife and his children, without anyone knowing.
He withdrew to another place.
When the criminals learned that they had gone away, they hurried there at night and plundered his house.
They left absolutely nothing behind, whether gold, silver, or clothing.
After all these losses and sorrows, they were robbed of their entire livelihood and everything they possessed.
All these things happened through the plotting of the adversary.
On that day, the whole populace was celebrating, and they were rejoicing over their victory against the Persians.
The king was celebrating with them amid great festivities.
It would have been fitting for Eustathius too to feast with them.
Since he was a high-ranking general in the Roman senate, the emperor searched for him but did not find him.
When the emperor learned that in a single hour nothing remained to him of all that he owned,
and that neither he nor those with him could be found,
the emperor and the entire senate were deeply grieved over him.
They were amazed at what had happened to him.
Then his wife said to him, “How long are we going to stay here?
Get up, and let us take our children who remain to us and go away, leaving this country behind, because we have become a laughingstock to those who know us.”
That night they took their children and set out to go to Egypt.
After they had traveled for a day or two, they came to the sea.
They found a ship moored at the harbor and asked to board it.
The captain of the ship was a savage barbarian.
After they boarded the ship, they set sail.
The captain saw that Eustathius’s wife had a very beautiful face, and he fell in love with her.
When he reached the seashore, he demanded his fare from him, but he had nothing there to pay.
He seized his wife because of the fare.
For this was the scheme he had devised against him, so that he would not return her to her husband.
Eustathius spent a long time speaking with him and pleading with him. The captain signaled to the sailors to seize him and throw him into the sea.
When Eustathius realized their plot, he unwillingly left his wife behind, took his two children, and walked away with them, weeping.
He lamented, saying, “Woe to me, my children! Your mother has been taken away by a barbarian.”
As he walked, he sighed and wept. He came to a river, and because of the great quantity of water in the channels,
he was unable to carry his two children across at the same time.
He put one on his neck.
He left the other on this side of the water.
He crossed the water and set down on the bank the one he had carried.
He turned back for the other.
While he was in the middle of the river,
he looked and saw a lion that had seized his child. It carried him off and went away.
His father hurried after him.
Then he turned back, still having hope for the other one.
Again he saw that the other one had been snatched away by a wolf.
When he saw that his children had been taken captive by wild beasts,
he tore at the hair on his head.
He mourned bitterly in great anguish.
He began to throw himself into the sea.
But God's care strengthened his heart so that he would understand what was going to happen to him.
He did not do this, but crossed the water to go into the wilderness.
Some shepherds saw the little boy in the lion's mouth, unharmed.
They said plainly, “It is God's providence that guards this little boy
and helps him and rescues him from the wild beast.”
They chased after the lion with their dogs.
The lion became afraid.
By God's arrangement, the lion dropped the little boy.
It ran away, and the shepherds picked up the little boy and raised him as their own child on the eastern side of the river.
As for the other one, whom the wolf had seized,
God's providence protected him from harm.
When some farmers saw him, they ran and took him away from the wolf. He had suffered no harm at all.
The farmers and the shepherds lived in the same village.
They took the little children and raised them in their homes.
But Eustathius knew nothing of what had happened.
Instead, he walked along weeping and saying words like these: “Woe to me!
I once flourished like a tree.
But now I have dried up and withered.”
Woe to me! I was once exalted, but now I am like a captive. Woe to me! I once had multitudes of soldiers under me, but now you have left me alone.
They did not even leave me my wife and my children.
But do not abandon me forever, Lord.
And do not forget my tears.
Lord, you told me, “You must be tested like Job.”
And look, I see that the suffering has become far greater.
Although they stripped that man of his possessions, they left him the dung heap to sit on.
But I will be a miserable stranger, bearing this multitude of hardships.
Job, for his part, had his children there comforting him.
And they were suffering with him.
But the wild beasts have taken away from me the comfort of my children.

Although that man's branches were cut off—I mean his children—he could see that his root remained with him, namely his wife. She was a comfort to him, even though, as a woman, she stumbled in something she said.
But as for me, this poor man, my root has been torn out on every side.
I see no ray of light from the lamp of my family.
Instead, I am like a tree in the desert, shaken at every moment by the devil's wind.
Do not be angry, Lord; do not distress your servant who speaks so much.
I say these inappropriate things because I am distressed at heart.
So, Lord, set a guard at my mouth and a secure door before my lips, so that my heart will not turn aside to evil words,
and you cast me out of your presence. So give me relief, Lord.
While he was saying these things, sighing and weeping, he came to a village called Bassus.
He entered it and worked there, earning his daily food.
After he had lived there a long time, the people of that village asked him to go and guard the crops in the fields. He spent ten years doing this and receiving his wages.
His children were brought up in the village we mentioned earlier, and they did not know that they were brothers.
Meanwhile, the shipowner who had taken Eustathius's wife brought her to his homeland.
A great shadow from God overshadowed her, so that the barbarian could [?] touch her throughout that time.
For this was what that woman had asked of God: that he would not let that foreigner touch her at all.
After that barbarian died, she remained in that place. After some days, those foreign peoples among whom Eustathius’s wife was living rose up and set out to seize the Romans’ territory.
Emperor Trajan was deeply distressed because of the war with the foreign peoples. He remembered Placidus, especially his strength and his many victories over the foreign peoples.
The memory of Eustathius stirred within him.
He was bewildered by the change that had suddenly come over him.
So he considered the war and consulted with the soldiers in his kingdom.
He was deeply grieved about Placidus and discussed with the soldiers whether Placidus was still alive.
He said, “Whoever reports, ‘I have found him,’ I will give him great honor and allowances, and make him very rich.”
Two of his soldiers, one named Antiochus and the other Acacius, had served Eustathius continually when he was with them.
They went to look for him and searched almost the entire kingdom until they reached the village where Eustathius was.
As they were walking through the places Eustathius was guarding, he saw them from a distance.
He recognized them by the way they walked.
He remembered his former way of life and began to grieve.
He prayed, saying, “Lord God, merciful one, who saves everyone who hopes in him, just as I have unexpectedly seen those who formerly traveled with me,
now, then, command that you look down upon me and your servant, who is my wife.
For I know that my children have become food for wild animals because of my evil deeds. Grant that I too may see them at the resurrection.”
While Eustathius was still saying these things, he heard a voice saying to him, “Take courage, Eustathius. In due time,
you will be restored to your former position, and you will receive your wife and your children.
At the resurrection of the dead, you will see the everlasting good things.
So do not deny me, and you will find undisturbed rest, and your name will grow greater through every generation.”
When he heard these things, he was afraid and walked down through the place where he was.
He stood near them on the road, in front of them.
He recognized them with certainty, but they did not recognize him.
They said to him, “Hello, friend!” He, in turn,
said to them, “Peace to you, my brothers.”
They said to him, “Do you know a stranger here called Placidus, together with his wife and his children?
If you tell us about him, we will give you a great deal of money.”
He said to them, “For what reason are you looking for him?”
They said to him, “He is our friend, and we have wanted to meet him for many years.”
He said to them, “I do not know the man.”
“Then make yourselves comfortable with me, for it is getting late. Rest with me here in the place where I am staying.”
“For I too am a stranger.”
And he took them into his house.
He went to buy some wine for them to drink.
He said to the owner of the house where he was, “I know these men.
That is why they have come to me here. So give me some food and wine, so that they can rest here with me, and I will pay you their cost when I receive my wages.”
The man gladly gave him everything he had available.
Eustathius continued serving them. He could not bear it as he thought back on his former life, but he restrained himself from crying.
He went outside, cried, and washed his face.
He went inside and served them again. And he saw him again.
They gradually began to recognize him, and they spoke to one another, saying, “This man looks like the one we are looking for.”
The other said to his companion, “Yes, he looks like him. But I know of a mark on his neck from when he was wounded in the war against the Massagetae.
Let us watch him carefully to see whether he has this mark or not.
If it is on his neck, then he is that man.”
When they looked carefully for the mark, they saw the scar on his neck.
Immediately they got up and kissed him.
They asked him, “Are you Placidus, the great general of former times?”
But he denied it, saying, “No,” and restrained himself from crying.
When they pointed out to him the scar on his neck, they solemnly declared to him, “You are Placidus the general.” And they asked him about his wife and his children.
He said to them, “They have died.”
While he was still speaking with them about these things, they raised their voices and wept bitterly, until everyone in the village heard them.
While they were still crying out, the villagers came to see what had happened, and they were frightened and disturbed.
But the soldiers calmed the disturbance and told them about the man's valor and his former rank.
When the villagers heard these things, they sighed, saying, “Great is the rank of this man who became a hired worker for us!”
Then the soldiers reported the matter to the king, and they dressed him in fine clothes from among those they had with them.
They took him and set out on the road.
Everyone in the village walked with him, seeing him off.
But he pleaded with them and let them go.
While he was walking along the road with the soldiers, he told them what he had seen, how he had seen Christ, and also that he had been named Eustathius.
He told them everything that had happened to him. After they had spent ten days traveling along the road, they came to Emperor Trajan.
They told him how they had found Placidus.
Emperor Trajan came out to meet him, embraced him, and wept very much.
He asked him why he had gone away.
He told Trajan and the whole senate what had happened to him, and about his wife and his children.
He also told them how the ship’s captain had taken his wife by force, and how they had been carried off by wild beasts. He told them about their suffering.
In short, they were all filled with great joy because they had found him alive. The emperor comforted him and made him commander of the army as before.
When Eustathius inspected the whole army, he realized that it would not be sufficient for the war against the barbarians.
He informed the emperor.
Emperor Trajan ordered recruits to be enlisted.
He wrote a letter of this kind to every city, directing them to recruit men and examine them to see whether they were suitable, and to make them soldiers.
When they went to the village where Eustathius’s children were, they enlisted Eustathius’s two sons, and the boys were handed over to them as recruits.
The people of that place testified about them that they were physically strong and handsome in appearance.
When Eustathius gathered all the recruits, he assigned them to the military units. He saw that the two young men were more handsome than all the others.
He appointed them to serve him, because he recognized their noble character through their manners.
In his kindness, he kept them with him. Their willingness drew them to him every day, so that he loved them even more.
He ordered them to eat with him at his table.
After this, he arranged the troops as he usually did.
He set out for war, and the country that the barbarians had seized before that day—
he freed those who had been taken captive in it.
He crossed the river called the Hydaspes, climbed to the heights, and advanced into the barbarians’ territory farther inland.
He defeated these others too and plundered the whole country.
Eustathius considered other plans through God’s providence, which was calling him to go down to the place where his wife was.
She had been protected from the beginning, as I said, from the violence of the ship’s captain and tyrant, through God’s care.
When that foreigner died, she withdrew on her own and lived in the garden of one of the people who lived there.
She made a tent for herself alone.
When the general reached that village and plundered it, he pitched his camp there for three days, resting with his army, since that place was suitable for rest.
He also stayed in that garden where his wife was. The two sons, for their part, lodged in their mother's tent.
When noon came, they sat down and told each other about the events of their childhood. For they did not know that their mother was in that place, nor did they know what had happened to them.
Their mother was sitting there, listening to what they were saying.
The older brother said to the younger, “From the time of my childhood, I remember nothing except this: my father was a general, and my mother was a very beautiful woman. He had two sons.
“One was younger than I was. He had curly hair and a handsome face.
“They took us and brought us out of our house at night.
They boarded a ship with us. I did not know where we were going.
“When we came ashore from the ship, my mother stayed on the ship alone. I do not know why. But our father picked up both of us and walked away weeping.
“When he came to a river, he crossed it with my younger brother.
“But he left me on this side of the water.
“As he was about to return to carry me over, a lion sprang after me, picked me up, and carried me into the wilderness.
“Some shepherds were tending sheep in that place. They rescued me from the lion and raised me there.
“That is what I know. I do not know what happened to my younger brother and my father.”
When he heard these things from his older brother, he threw himself down and wept. He said, “You are my brother!
“I realized from what you said that you are my lord and brother. For I too was raised by shepherds, and they told me, ‘We rescued you from a wolf.’”
He embraced him, and they kissed each other.
While their mother was still listening to these things, she realized that they were her sons from what they had said about her remaining at sea on the ship.
She was saying to herself, “Are these my sons or not?
“Do my sons look like this?”
Nevertheless, she was deeply distressed, and her insides were shaken as she watched the boys embracing each other and weeping.
She kept watching them, saying, “Could they be my sons?” This was especially because they had said that their father was a general and that their mother had stayed on the ship.
The next day she approached the general, saying, “I beg you, my lord. I am a woman from the land of the Romans. They took me captive and brought me here.
“So I ask you: take me to my homeland.”
While she was still saying these things, she began to recognize him as her husband by the distinguishing marks she knew on him. When she recognized him, she was afraid to question him.
When she could no longer bear it, she fell down before him, saying, “I beg you, my lord, do not be angry with me.”
For I want you to tell me about your former way of life [?].
I too think that you are Placidus, the general whose name was changed to Eustace when you were baptized in the name of Christ Jesus, who revealed himself to you through an animal without reason.
You believed in him. And when you fell into the trials that the Lord had foretold to you, you took your wife, who is myself, and your two sons, Agapius and Theopistus.
You set out for Egypt. When we reached the sea, we boarded the ship, set out, sailed, and set out.
You lost me to the barbarian ship captain. He seized me.
He took me to his homeland. But the Lord Jesus Christ is my witness that neither that man nor anyone else defiled my body. Instead, I have preserved my chastity until now.
Now, if you are Eustace, as I have recognized you by the signs I have told you, I adjure you by the power of Christ: tell me, and hide nothing.
When Eustace heard these things, he was utterly amazed.
He looked at her features and recognized her, and great joy came over him.
He got up and immediately hurried to her. He said to her, “I am Eustathius, the one being spoken of.” And they kissed one another with a spiritual kiss.
They shed many tears and gave glory to God, who always does good to his servants and delivers them from all their afflictions.
His wife said to him, “Where are my children?”
He said to her, weeping, “Wild beasts carried them away.” And he told her what had happened to them while they were with him.
She said, “Let us give thanks to the Lord. For perhaps, just as he has graciously restored us to one another, he will also graciously restore our sons to us.”
Eustace said to her, “I have already told you that wild beasts carried them away.”
She answered, saying, “Yesterday, while I was still sitting in the garden, I heard two young men talking with one another about their childhood experiences and recounting what had happened to them.”
“I recognized them as our sons. But they did not know one another until the older one's words gave the younger one a sign by which to recognize him.
So, if you have remained unaware of this until now, understand that God's mercy has graciously restored us to one another.
Call them yourself and question them, and they will tell you.”
The general called the two young men and asked them, “Whose sons are you, and what happened to you in your childhood?”
They in turn told him what had happened to them, and immediately he recognized that they truly were his sons.
He embraced them wholeheartedly and kissed them.
The two of them fell upon their sons' necks.
They wept for an hour and thanked the Lord for their marvelous reunion.
The news of what had happened to them reached all the people of the city.
They gathered in one place, marveling and rejoicing at their reunion.
They rejoiced even more over the victory over the barbarians. That day they held a great feast to celebrate their recognition of one another.
The next day they called upon the Lord, raising their voices in thanksgiving for his great love for humanity.
After he had ravaged the territory of the barbarians, they returned with great joy, bringing with them a great quantity of plunder and many captives.
When Eustathius returned from the war, Emperor Trajan died.
Another king, whose name was Hadrian, took his place. He was exceedingly impious, more so than all the kings who had come before him.
When Eustathius returned from the war, the emperor came out to meet him, according to the custom of the Roman emperors.
He brought all his high officials with him to celebrate the victory over all the places Eustathius had captured.
Because of the bravery he had learned of, and because Eustathius had found his wife and children, he rejoiced even more.
When he came to the city, the emperor went ahead and entered the temple of Apollo. Eustathius did not go inside with him, but remained outside.

The emperor called him and asked him, “Why did you not come into the temple of Apollo and offer sacrifices to the gods, now that you have won and returned from the war, and send up sacrifices of thanksgiving to them, especially since you have found your wife and children?”
Eustathius said to the emperor, “I myself will offer our supplication and prayer, and many prostrations, to my king, Christ Jesus, because he had mercy on my misery and brought us out of captivity.
And it is he who gave me my wife and children. He helped us just as he told me he would before I received baptism in his name.
So now I know no other god besides him.
For he is God, who created heaven and earth, who alone performs these great wonders.”
Then the emperor became angry when he heard these things from Eustathius.
He had him brought before him as a civilian, together with his wife and children.
He spoke to them with frightening words and threats.
But the saints paid no attention and were not shaken at all.
When the emperor saw their steadfastness and their faith in Christ, he ordered them to be taken to the arena and a large lion to be released against them.
When the lion advanced toward them, it stopped beside the saints, bent its knees, and bowed before them. It also lowered its head before them.
Afterward it came out of the arena and went away.
When the emperor saw this extraordinary spectacle—that the wild beast had not touched them—he was bewildered.
He ordered a bronze bull to be made so that they could throw the saints into it and light a fire beneath them.
The crowd gathered to see the saints’ ordeal and the spectacle.
They were being brought out by means of the mechanisms of the apparatus, to be thrown into it.
The blessed Eustathius pleaded with the executioners to let them pray.
He stretched out his hands, together with his wife and children.

They prayed, saying, “Lord, God of hosts, whom no one sees, but whom we have seen according to his will, hear us now as we cry out to you. Let our prayer be fulfilled for us with one mind, in the confession of your name and your holy faith.”
And make us worthy to be counted among the holy martyrs, like the three holy young men whom you tested by fire and who did not deny you.
In the same way, accept us too in this fire as a sacrifice pleasing to you, as we become a burnt offering in the fire.
Grant favor, Lord, and a gracious gift to our bodies, so that everyone who remembers us may receive a gracious gift in the kingdom of heaven, and also rest on earth.
Even if they are in danger at sea or in the rivers, if they call upon your holy name, save them from their danger.
If those burdened with many sins bow down before you in our name, forgive their sins. And be a helper, Lord, to everyone who remembers us on the day bearing our name.
May the threat of the fire surrounding us become refreshing dew for us, so that, Lord, our bodies may not become hardened in it.
As they said these things in prayer, they heard a voice from heaven saying, “Just as you have been mighty champions in this life,
You have endured many trials. Now, then, do not be afraid. Come up to this place in peace and receive the imperishable crown.
you shall enjoy forever the good things prepared for you, in return for the sufferings you experienced and the trials you endured for a short time.”
When the saints heard these things, they willingly surrendered themselves with joy. The soldiers threw them into the bronze apparatus.
When they were thrown in, the flame of the fire surrounded them. They gave glory to the Holy Trinity, to whom victory belongs.
After a little while, they entrusted their souls into God's hands. The fire did not touch their bodies at all, nor even the hair on their heads.
After three days, the impious emperor Hadrian came to the place where the saints had met their end.
He ordered them to open the bronze bull so that he could see what had happened to the saints.
When they opened it, they found the saints' bodies intact, with no damage in them. They thought that they were alive.
And when they brought them out, they laid them on the ground. Great fear and amazement seized everyone standing around them, and the bodies of the saints shone like snow.
When the defiled Hadrian saw them, he was astonished and afraid, and he withdrew.
The crowd standing there also cried out, saying, “You are great, Lord, God of the Christians!

You alone are the great, true God, Jesus Christ, and there is no other besides you, because you did not allow evil to touch the saints' bodies. Instead, they shone even more brightly, radiant with glory and joy.”
When evening came, the Christians came and took the bodies of the holy martyrs. They secretly placed them in an honored place in the city of Rome.
And after the persecution [?], they also built a martyrs’ shrine for them, celebrating in it with hymns and songs of praise, according to the custom of the Christians.
They commemorate the holy repose of these honored martyrs on the twentieth day of the month of December, which is Thoth in the language of the Egyptians.
This is the life and struggle of these blessed holy martyrs: Saint Apa Eustathius, Apa Agapius and Apa Theopistus, his sons, and Amma Theopiste, his wife.
This is the completion of their honored struggle.

Everyone, therefore, who is worthy to celebrate their holy commemoration and calls upon them will obtain the good things of the kingdom of heaven through the grace and love for humanity of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom glory belongs to him, together with his good Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever.
Amen.
Victor, the least of deacons, son of the blessed Mer[?], a deacon.
